info.title: Handline daemon protocol
info.description: OpenRPC-shaped. Source of contract/protocol.md and contract/protocol.ts: regenerate with `python3 contract/generate.py`. Extensions are x-* keys.

x-framing.reach: v1 reaches this machine, the LAN or Tailscale only (founder decision 3): the network listener binds the address the config names (default loopback; a LAN or Tailscale address is opt-in), always speaks an encrypted WebSocket whose certificate fingerprint is in the pairing QR, and has no relay or public endpoint.
transport: Unix socket (0600, owned by the local user; the role is proven by hello, not by the socket), one JSON-RPC 2.0 object per line
WebSocket (network listener, off by default), one object per text frame
x-framing.lines: UTF-8 JSON, terminated by \n, at most 1 MiB. No batches (bad_request). A connection may carry many calls; a one-shot call works.
x-framing.ids: Request id is the client's integer or string; replies may arrive in any order. Notifications (no id) flow from the daemon after subscribe or terminal.attach, interleaved with replies.
x-framing.concurrency: Calls on one connection are served concurrently: a call that waits (inbox.list or inbox.get with wait_s, up to 600 s) does not hold up the calls after it, and replies come in the order they finish, matched by id. Calls on one connection that touch the same thing are not ordered by the connection: a client that needs the order waits for the first reply. Stream notifications are never held behind a waiting call.
x-framing.network: The network listener is the only way in for a phone, a browser or another machine, and only a paired device may use it. A connection on it is unpaired until its hello carries a valid device `token`. An unpaired connection may call device.redeem and nothing else: every other call, hello and an unknown method name included, is refused before any handler runs with the one reply `{code: -32002, message: "refused", data: {code: "refused", gate: "unpaired", reason: "not paired"}}`, the same words every time: no method list, no state, no version, no hint, nothing that says why. A token that is revoked or was never issued is the same refusal, so a reply does not say which. The Unix socket is not the network: its roles are proven as below. Conformance: the network transport is the WebSocket over TLS the listener speaks, and a client pins the certificate fingerprint from the pairing uri; fixtures with `as: unpaired` or `as: member` over the network are run against it with `--as unpaired=...` and `--as member=...` sockets that are already past TLS and the pinned check (a socket the harness is given, or a connector function); contract/README.md says what that does and does not show.
x-framing.legacy: A line with `verb` and no `jsonrpc` is a legacy request, answered {ok, said} by the adapter until its last caller has moved.
x-framing.request_id: Every write takes request_id. The daemon keeps each successful reply for 24 hours; a retry with the same id and the same params returns it with replayed:true and repeats nothing. The same id with other params is bad_request. Refusals and errors are not stored: a retry is judged again. One exception: chat.send to a structured agent returns the receipt as it is now (see x-delivery).
x-framing.unknown_method: A method the daemon does not know is JSON-RPC error -32601 with data.code `bad_request` and data.method; a method it knows but the caller's role may not call is `refused`, gate `role`.
x-framing.idle: A line begun but not finished within 30 s is dropped with bad_request, and so is a connection that has not said hello within 30 s. After hello, a connection with nothing in flight is closed after 3600 s without a byte. A subscribed or terminal-attached connection has no idle limit (the daemon notices a dead peer by a failed write); the subscribe and terminal tasks must build that. A call that waits (inbox wait_s) is in flight.

x-handshake: The first call is hello. Compatibility: adding a method or field never changes protocol; removing or changing one does, and the daemon then serves old and new side by side for one release. Clients ignore unknown fields and unknown enum-like strings (state words, kinds, event types). A client that does not know the daemon's protocol refuses to run and prints the one command that fixes it: `hl service install`.

x-roles.rule: x-role on a method is the lowest role that may call it. Roles are proven, not assumed. founder: the connection said hello with the founder key and it matches (a Unix-socket peer being the same user proves nothing, because agents run as that user). agent: the peer pid verifies against a recorded session. member: a paired device's token. Anything else is anonymous: on the Unix socket it may call only hello and device.redeem; on the network listener it is unpaired and may call only device.redeem (see Framing, network). A call below its role is refused, gate `role`. session.type and session.keys act at a shell prompt as they do anywhere in the pane: only a paired device can connect to the network listener and an unpaired caller gets no data, so a shell is within what a paired device may reach.

x-gates.role: Caller's role is agent: a person-at-the-terminal method.
x-gates.terminal_lock: The agent's terminal lock, the one the tick holds.
x-gates.input_holder: Someone else holds the input. A daemon holder is a short hold, not a refusal.
x-gates.wall: The usage limit (wall_reason): typing would only spend quota.
x-gates.screen_blocker: A dialog is open, so a typed line would answer it. Use keys or prompt.answer.
x-gates.state: The state checks the legacy verb has today; this protocol adds none.
x-gates.unsupported: The host or the format cannot do it: a resize on a host that cannot, bytes on a terminal whose host serves only text. transcript.events for an agent the daemon runs as a terminal; the typing and terminal methods for an agent it runs as a structured session.
x-gates.not_self: The agent named is not the caller's own session.
x-gates.attempt_limit: Too many wrong pairing codes: five wrong tries kill a code, and five wrong codes in ten minutes from one address refuse device.redeem from it for fifteen minutes.
x-gates.unpaired: A network connection with no valid device token called anything but device.redeem. The reply is always message "refused" and reason "not paired": no data, no method list, no version, no hint. A revoked token is refused the same way, and its connections are closed.
x-gates.pairing_code: device.redeem: the code is wrong, expired or already used. The reply does not say which.
x-gates.session_token: Session token and peer-pid check, unchanged.
x-gates.proposal_changed: hr.decide: the proposal changed after the caller read it (its `subject` is no longer the one handed in). Checked after the settled check. Nothing was done; the refusal's `proposal` is the proposal as it is now, to be read and decided again.
x-gates.proposal_settled: hr.decide, hr.withdraw: the proposal is already approved, rejected or withdrawn, so there is nothing to decide or take back. The refusal's `proposal` is the proposal as it is now.
x-gates.confirm: chat.cancel: the message was delivered, so cancelling needs confirm true. data.plan says what it would do.

x-note-topics: The plan's earlier `requests` topic is replaced by `chat` (messages and landing state) and `inbox` (decisions); `usage` by `accounts`. The `hr` topic: hr.raised: a proposal was raised (state open); one event per proposal, once. hr.settled: a proposal left open or its apply ran again: it was decided, withdrawn, or its apply failed; sent for every outcome, a retry of an apply_failed one that fails again included (state apply_failed, a new error); the Proposal carries the new state and `settled`. The event's `agent` is the proposal's agent (null for a bundle), `title` its title, `target` {screen: hr, id: the proposal's id as text}, and `data` {proposal: the whole Proposal}, so a client updates its list and its count without a refetch; a client that missed events refetches hr.list. What hr.list serves, and in which order: see its description. An edit of a draft in place (the file is writable by its author) sends no event: a card learns of it from the refusal proposal_changed.

x-identity.rule: x-callers on a method, when present, lists the only roles that may call it, whatever the chain says. The agent-identity methods (hook.record, agent.set, task.progress, land, land.pass, land.authorize) act as the caller's OWN session, found by peer pid or session token as say already finds its sender: an `agent` argument that is not the caller's own name is refused (gate not_self), and a member device cannot call them (agent.set is also the founder's, who may name any agent).
x-identity.sender: say and task.new carry no sender parameter: the daemon sets it. An agent's calls carry its own name; a member device's and the founder's carry `human`.
x-identity.ownership: Methods that act on a request or task by id (withdraw, edit, release, discard, merge, memo.edit, memo.delete, queue, draft) keep today's checks on who may: the opener, the owner, the owner's manager or the founder; a refusal is `refused` with the reason.

x-dropped-from-agents.note: Agent commands the spec does not keep at agent role, for the founder to decide. Each is founder-only or a person's act today, or is not a daemon call.
founder_only_today: hl account add|remove|register|cap|cycle|recover (set; the billing-cycle and cap reads are for the next spec task)
hl device pair|list|revoke (device.pair, devices.list, device.revoke: the gateway's socket, from the founder's terminal)
needs_a_decision: hl spawn (a founder's act; no method serves it)
hl agent register (a roster change, founder)

x-state-words.rule: AgentView.state is one of these lower-case words. The set is open: a client treats a word it does not know as idle and keeps working. Upper case is never sent: the daemon's internal states (IDLE, QUEUED, RUNNING, DONE, HANDOFF, DEGRADED, PARKED, THROTTLED, STALLED) and the view words its screens use (PENDING, MOVING, DIALOG, FATAL) are mapped to these before they leave it. The mapping is made from the source facts (the state row, its wake time, the screen), never by reading state_detail text.

words.running: A turn is running (a hand-off in progress counts: moving is working).
words.idle: At its prompt with nothing to do, or nothing pending for it (a park with no work behind it, a finished one). state_detail may say what it waits on (a child task, background work).
words.queued: Has work and will start at the daemon's next tick, with no time to wait for. state_detail may say why it is not running yet (a restart retry).
words.parked: Waits for a time: the usage window rolling over, a park a person asked for, a throttle or degraded retry, or an account move settling. state_detail is the clock (`due` once it has passed; `moving` for an account move, which has no clock).
words.waiting: A person must answer: a dialog or a prompt is open (has_dialog is true).
words.stalled: Stopped until a person unstalls it (the daemon will not wake it).
words.blocked: Reserved: waiting on a blocker the view names in `block`. The daemon does not send it today; a client draws it as blocked.
words.no_terminal: Registered but with no terminal to show: never started or its terminal closed, and nothing waits for it. Checked before idle; a closed agent with work waiting is queued or parked.

x-state-words.pending: PENDING is two words, by what it waits for: `queued` when nothing but the next tick stands between it and a start, `parked` when it waits for a time. A client draws both as waiting its turn, and the clock in state_detail tells them apart. MOVING is `parked` with state_detail `moving`.

x-dialogs.rule: A dialog in an agent's terminal is routine, a human's or unknown. The daemon answers only the routine ones, and only at launch, once, from what the founder already decided; it never answers any other (no key into a pane after launch). A human's dialog and an unknown one are `needs_you` on the agent (AgentView), and the person answers them at the terminal terminal.open points to. Unknown is a person: a dialog the table does not name is class human, kind dialog. The class is decided from the hook or session file that reported it, never from the screen, except the two launch screens, which the launch reads once.

folder_trust.answered_by: the folder is inside a declared trust root (standing consent, trust.*)

bypass_warning.answered_by: the agent's mode is bypass and the founder granted it

tool_permission.reported_by: PermissionRequest hook; Notification permission_prompt; the session file needs

question.reported_by: Notification elicitation_dialog; the session file needs

usage_limit_choice.reported_by: the session file needs; Stop with a limit

exit_confirm.note: The daemon ends a session by stopping its process, never by typing /exit, so the dialog does not arise; if one is there anyway it is human, kind dialog.

startup_notice.note: Any other screen a launch stops at (new MCP servers, an update, a login). Not answered; the launch reports needs_you.

x-dialogs.retired: Dialog rules (answer.add with vendor, title and label; the `dialog` entries of answers.list; the auto_accept_dialogs setting) answered a dialog by matching its screen. A daemon that never answers a dialog and reads no screen refuses to save one (gate unsupported), lists none and ignores the setting; the Python daemon, which still runs agents, keeps serving them until the cutover. Trust roots are not rules and stay.

event.note: Sent after subscribe, for the subscribed topics, in cursor order.

gap.note: retention: the resume cannot be served (the cursor is older than the daemon keeps, or more than 5000 of the subscribed events behind); refetch the topic's snapshot; the connection stays open and the cursor is the newest. slow_client: more than 1000 live events were waiting to be written to this client; the daemon sends this and then closes the connection. A resume up to 5000 behind is replayed in full and does not count toward the 1000. The daemon sets no `topic` in v1.

format.description: Present on a `styled` attach's frames and absent on a text one's, so a connection that watches one terminal in both formats can tell which attach a frame belongs to.

frame.note: Text and styled attaches only. full:true carries every line and is what a slow client gets instead of a backlog. A frame may carry `changed: []` for a cursor move alone.

resize.note: Text attaches only; a bytes attach gets a snapshot notice instead.

format.description: The attach this notice belongs to, whose counter `seq` is: a terminal watched in both formats is sent each of these twice. Additive: a client that does not know it ignores it.

marker.note: The daemon typed, or a control call happened, at this point in the stream.

format.description: The attach this notice belongs to, whose counter `seq` is: a terminal watched in both formats is sent each of these twice. Additive: a client that does not know it ignores it.

holder.note: Sent to attached clients whenever the holders change (take, release, the idle hold timeout, the daemon taking over for a send). agent.changed carries the same in AgentView.input_holders.

data.description: Base64 of what the program wrote.

output.note: Bytes attaches only: the pane's output in order, at most one notice per 50 ms and 64 KiB decoded each. A notice may end inside a multi-byte character or an escape sequence.

data.description: Base64, as in the attach snapshot.

snapshot.note: Bytes attaches only: the screen again, to be repainted as after an attach (reset, resize to cols by rows, write data), because the terminal changed size or the client fell behind. Everything the stream would have said before it is dropped; output follows with the next seq.

x-terminal: Format `text` sends plain text rows (frame notices). Format `styled` sends the same rows and frames with each row's style runs (Row.spans), for a host that has no byte stream or a client that cannot run a terminal emulator (below). Format `bytes` (below) sends the pane's own escape-coded output, which carries the colour. One poller per terminal, at most ~5 reads a second however many clients; it stops when the last client leaves. The input holders are a list (TerminalSnapshot.holders, AgentView.input_holders) with a `holder` notice on change; a holder that has not typed for the input_hold_idle_s setting loses the hold.

x-terminal-bytes.format: `terminal.attach` and `terminal.history` take `format`: `text` (the default; what they send is unchanged) or `bytes`. The format belongs to the attach, so two clients may watch one terminal in different formats. `hello.capabilities.terminal_format` lists the formats the daemon serves at all and `terminal_hosts` maps each host it has to its formats, e.g. `{tmux: [text, bytes], orca: [text]}`. A bytes request for a terminal whose host cannot serve it is refused, gate `unsupported`, and nothing is attached; a client then asks for text. A `format` that is neither word is bad_request naming `format`. A connection has at most one attach per terminal and format (see terminal.attach); detach takes an optional `format`.
x-terminal-bytes.encoding: Bytes travel as base64 (standard alphabet, padded) in JSON strings on the same transport as every other message: no binary frames. They need not be valid UTF-8, and a notice may end inside a character or an escape sequence, so a client writes each as bytes to a terminal that keeps its own parser state.
x-terminal-bytes.snapshot: `data` is written unchanged to a freshly reset terminal of `cols` by `rows` (the client resizes, resets, writes, in one step). It begins with `ESC [ ? 1049 h` when `alt_screen` is true, then paints the visible rows with their SGR codes, each row ending in a reset and rows separated by CR LF, never a bare LF; then sets the modes the pane has on that change what a client sends (application cursor keys, bracketed paste, mouse reporting and its SGR encoding) as far as the host reports them; it ends by placing the cursor at `cursor` and showing or hiding it as `cursor_visible` says. It is at most 1 MiB decoded: a screen whose coded form is larger is sent with its styling left out, never refused. Later transitions of the alternate screen are in the stream; the flag is for the snapshot alone.
x-terminal-bytes.sequence: One counter per attach, shared by all its notices (`output`, `snapshot`, `marker`, `holder`), and it goes up by exactly 1 with each. The snapshot's `seq` is the last notice its screen includes: the daemon takes the screen and starts the stream together, so the first notice after the reply has `seq` + 1 and no byte is lost or repeated between them. A client ignores a notice whose seq is not above the last it applied and re-attaches on a hole. The counters of different attaches, text ones included, are unrelated: a connection that watches one terminal in both formats has two counters, and attaching the same terminal and format again replaces that attach and starts a new one at its snapshot's seq. There is no resume: after a reconnect the client attaches again and repaints from the new snapshot, and what it missed is not replayed.
x-terminal-bytes.slow_client: Output is never dropped from the middle. When one attach's unsent output reaches 1 MiB decoded, the daemon discards all of it and sends one `snapshot` notice, reason `slow_client`, with a seq above everything discarded; output follows it. Counting bytes, not seconds, is the whole rule. A connection that falls behind on events past the gap rule is closed with gap `slow_client` as before and attaches again.
x-terminal-bytes.history: Lines come as strings with their SGR codes, as the host keeps them: one physical row each (the row as the pane wrapped it, never joined), starting at default attributes and ending in a reset, with no line break inside. `history` on attach and `limit` on `terminal.history` count lines as in text (default 100, at most 2000); a page is trimmed to 1 MiB and says `more`. Only the normal screen has scrollback: while `alt_screen` is true the snapshot's history is empty.
x-terminal-bytes.input: `terminal.input` carries keystrokes and pasted bytes as base64; its gates and recording are on the method.
x-terminal-bytes.resize: `terminal.resize` is unchanged: the input holder alone, restored when they leave. A bytes attach is told of any size change, the holder's or the restore, by a `snapshot` notice, reason `resize`, with the new cols and rows, and gets no `resize` notice: the client repaints rather than reflow, as tmux's reflow is not xterm's.
x-terminal-bytes.markers: `marker` and `holder` notices come to a bytes attach as to a text one, in the one counter: a `marker` stands where the daemon typed, before the output that echoes it. Each carries `format`, the attach it was sent to, since a terminal watched in both formats gets each notice once per attach with that attach's counter.

x-terminal-styled.format: `terminal.attach` and `terminal.history` take `format: styled`. It is the text format with colour: the snapshot has `format` `styled`, every Row in `lines`, `history` and `terminal.history` pages may carry `spans`, and every `frame` notice of the attach carries `format` `styled`. Frames, seq, `full`, `changed`, `cursor` and `resize` are as for text; the `holder` and `marker` notices are as for text too, and carry `format` `styled` on this attach so a client can tell its counter from a text attach's of the same terminal, and `text` is exactly what a text attach would send. Offered the way `bytes` is: `hello.capabilities.terminal_format` lists it and `terminal_hosts` maps each host to its formats, e.g. `{tmux: [text, bytes, styled], orca: [text]}` (`orca` joins it only when its screen read exposes attributes, see `when`); a styled request for a terminal whose host cannot serve it is refused, gate `unsupported`, and nothing is attached; a client then asks for text. The format belongs to the attach, so a text and a styled attach of one terminal on one connection have unrelated counters. `terminal.detach` takes `styled` as it takes `bytes`.
x-terminal-styled.when: A host serves `styled` when its rendered-screen read gives the attributes of each cell, not only the characters. It is meant for the Orca host, whose CLI has no byte stream (`bytes` would need a raw output stream, the modes, the alternate screen and the cursor from Orca, none of which `orca terminal read` offers) but does render the screen it reads (`--screen`). Whether that read exposes cell attributes is not yet shown: `orca terminal read --help` says nothing of them, so Orca serves `styled` only once its screen read does, which is an open request to Orca. The phone app has no terminal emulator and uses the format on any host that serves it. A host whose read has no attributes stays `text`: the daemon never invents styles, and never sends `spans` on a terminal that has none to give.
x-terminal-styled.spans: A run is `[from, to)` over the row's characters counted in Unicode code points of `text` (not UTF-16 units, not bytes; a client in JavaScript converts with `Array.from`), and may extend past the end of `text` for blank cells that have a background: past the end, each blank cell counts as one, so `to` is at most len(`text`) + (`cols` minus the display width of `text`), where a wide character (CJK) is one code point and two cells. A run boundary never falls inside a cell: a base character stays with its combining code points, and a wide character is one unit. Runs are sorted, never overlap, are never empty and are sent only for cells whose style is not the default; a cell no run covers is drawn default. Two neighbouring cells with the same style are one run. Style is `SpanStyle`: `fg`, `bg` (a palette index 0-255 or `#rrggbb`) and the flags `bold`, `dim`, `italic`, `underline`, `inverse`, `strike`, each left out when off. Palette indexes 0-15 are the client's theme colours, so a dark and a light client each draw them in their own tokens; the daemon does not resolve a colour it was given as an index.
x-terminal-styled.cursor: A frame's `cursor` (text and styled attaches; a bytes attach's is in cells) is `{x, y}` or null: null when the cursor is hidden or above the frame. `x` counts code points of the row's `text`, as spans do (a host that reads cells converts; a wide character is one), and may run past the end of `text` when the cursor sits in blank cells, each counting one. `y` is a row of the frame's `lines`, from 0, and may be len(lines) or more when the cursor is on a blank row the frame drops. A frame may carry `changed: []` for a cursor move alone.
x-terminal-styled.size: A row's spans are what its colours need and no more; `terminal.history` pages and the 1 MiB trim of a text page apply to the JSON as sent, spans included, and `more` says when it was trimmed. A frame for a screen of a few hundred runs is a few KiB; the slow-client rule of text is unchanged (`full: true`).
x-terminal-styled.input: `styled` is read-only like text: keys go by `terminal.input` where the host supports bytes in, and by `session.type` and `session.keys` as before.
x-terminal-styled.not_in_it: No hyperlink, image, blink or font-weight beyond bold, no wide-character marker beyond what `text` has, no mouse or screen-mode state: a client that needs the real terminal asks for `bytes`.

methods.name: hello
methods.summary: First call on every connection: versions and who the caller is.

schema.description: name/version of the caller.
The protocol the client will speak.
Device token; network listener only.
The founder key, from the founder's own key file; local socket only. Wrong key: refused, gate `role`.

min_client.description: Oldest client protocol it still serves.

methods.description: A client whose protocol is below min_client gets `refused` (gate `protocol`) with hint `hl service install`. A newer client gets a normal reply and decides itself whether to run. Any other call before hello is bad_request. Role by proof: a matching `key` gives founder; with no key, a peer pid that verifies against a recorded session gives agent; a device token (network listener) gives member; anything else is anonymous and every method but hello is refused until a later hello proves more. On the network listener a hello without a valid `token` is refused, gate `unpaired`, with no data; with one it is member.

methods.name: whoami
methods.summary: The viewer, the device, the role and the methods allowed.

methods.description: The same list hello gives, with allowed flags for this caller.

methods.name: subscribe
methods.summary: Turn the connection into a stream of `event` notices; replays after `since` first.

schema.description: Last cursor seen. Absent: live only. A cursor older than the daemon keeps, or with more than 5000 subscribed events after it, is answered by a `gap` notice (reason retention) instead of a replay; the connection stays open. Up to 5000 events behind, every missed event is replayed in full, in cursor order, before any live one.
Only events of this agent, plus events that carry no agent. Meant for the chat topic.

cursor.description: The newest cursor at subscribe time.

methods.description: topics is a non-empty list of known topics, else -32602 bad_request naming `topics`. Notices start only after this reply is sent. devices is subscribed on its own, by the founder: a topics list naming devices and any other topic is -32602 bad_request naming `topics`, because devices is served by the gateway itself and every other topic by the daemon behind it. A devices subscription is live only: `since` and `agent` are ignored, the reply cursor is 0, its events carry cursor 0, and a client that reconnects reads devices.list again. The transcript topic needs member, as transcript.events does: an agent session that names it is refused, gate role, and nothing is subscribed (the stream holds every agent's tool inputs and results).

methods.name: unsubscribe
methods.summary: Stop some topics; a subscription with no topics left ends. Result {}.
methods.description: Naming devices follows the same rule as subscribe: on its own.

methods.name: daemon.status
methods.summary: Status bar: alive, versions, terminal host, agent counts, inbox count.

methods.name: events.feed
methods.summary: Resumable feed of events with their deep-link targets; the polling twin of subscribe.

gap.description: True when `since` is older than retention; refetch snapshots.

methods.description: topics defaults to [notifications]; limit defaults to 50, at most 200. Without `since`: the newest events, oldest first. With `since`: the events after it; if `since` is older than retention the feed starts at the oldest kept event and `gap` is true. cursor is the newest cursor in the reply, or the current newest when there are no events.

methods.name: operation.get
methods.summary: A long-running operation's current state.

methods.name: agents.list
methods.summary: The rail: the stored view of every agent.

schema.description: Add the status-line fields of each agent (started, has_repo, has_terminal, screen_word, screen_detail, unreached, task_waits, wake_wait_reason), read now and not from the stored view. Default false.

methods.name: agent.get
methods.summary: One agent: the view plus session and terminal facts.

methods.name: agent.timeline
methods.summary: The agent's recorded events, newest first.

schema.description: Return rows older than this id.
Default 50, at most 200.

methods.description: Today this is the agent's generic recorded events (the daemon's events table, rows of that agent): id is the event's id and `before` an event id; kind is the recorded kind; actor is the payload's `actor` when it is an object, else null; text is the payload's `text`, else `detail`, else `method`, else the kind; data is the whole payload ({} when it has none). State changes, deliveries and key presses appear only once they are recorded as events, which a later task does; clients must not expect them, and must treat kind as an open set.

methods.name: agent.options
methods.summary: What the new-agent form offers.

methods.name: agent.set
methods.summary: Change an agent's settings: an agent its own ordinary keys, the founder any (legacy agent_set).

methods.name: agent.fold
methods.summary: Run hl fold for an agent (legacy fold).

methods.name: agent.move
methods.summary: Move an agent to another account (legacy move).

methods.name: agent.unstall
methods.summary: Clear a STALLED agent: it goes to queued with its failure counters reset, as hl unstall does. Refused (gate state) when the agent is not stalled. Only a test daemon serves it; the real daemon does not list it, and an app then shows Clear stall off.

methods.name: session.start
methods.summary: Launch a session for the agent, optionally on a named account: in its terminal, or for a structured agent as a structured session with no terminal.

schema.description: The Go daemon does not place sessions on a named account yet: it answers bad_request, field account, never drops it. A client offers no account picker until then.

methods.name: session.wake
methods.summary: Resume a closed session.

methods.name: chat.send
methods.summary: A message to an agent through the daemon's delivery (queued, typed, landed); needs no input hold. With parent, a reply to a message. To a structured agent the request_id is the operation id and the result carries a receipt.

schema.description: The message this one replies to. When that message waits on the person (a question or a decision put to them, or an answer to what they asked) this is its answer, as chat.answer; otherwise it is a say to the agent under it. Not with task. A message that does not exist is not_found; one that agent is not on, as its requester or its target, is refused (gate state); a message between two other agents is replied to by a say to the one named by agent. request in the result is then the message replied to, for an answer, or the new message.

For a structured agent whose turn is running: now joins the running turn, queue (the default) is held by the daemon and written when the turn ends, one message per turn. With no turn running they are the same. A terminal agent accepts the field and ignores it. Another word is bad_request.

A repeat of an operation that was withdrawn is refused (gate state): a retry does not bring back what the person took back.

A terminal agent's message is as before.

methods.description: Without `state`: every proposal that waits (open, and apply_failed until it is decided again) and every settled one (approved, rejected, withdrawn) from the last 7 days, at most 50 of those. Order: the waiting ones first, oldest `created` first; then the settled ones, newest `settled` first. A client counts the dot from `open` and `apply_failed`. With `state`, only that state, in the same order, and no 7-day or 50 bound. A proposal whose requested_by is human is never listed: the founder made that change directly and was not asked (the bridge leaves it out of its cards too). The Python store's states map as: proposed = open; approved = apply_failed (it holds the founder's approval and the change is not applied: `error` is set when an apply ran and failed, null when it never ran, e.g. a crash between the two); applied = approved; rejected = rejected; withdrawn = withdrawn; enacting and failed exist only for a human's own change and are never listed.

Refused with gate `state` while the account is already logging in; not_found for an unknown account. The end of a login is not a method: the accounts topic reports it in the account's `login`.

methods.description: Idempotent: a login already ended answers accepted. An id the daemon never issued is not_found. The login's whole process group is killed, since the CLI ignores SIGTERM for a second.

schema.description: One-time; written to the CLI's stdin and nowhere else.

methods.description: The code is never echoed back, never in an event, a log or the request record. Refused with gate `state` when the login is not waiting for a code. An id the daemon never issued is not_found.

schema.description: Change nothing: answer `plan` and `would_remove`. A dry run needs no `confirm`.
The account's name, as the founder typed it; required unless dry_run.

The dialog's title; a long command's truncated title is refused.
The option label to choose.

methods.description: Blank fields add nothing; a half-filled rule is refused. Founder because the dialog-rule store and trust are the founder's alone: an agent that could write them could answer its own dialogs. methods.name: devices.list

methods.name: device.pair
methods.summary: Make a one-time pairing code.

schema.description: Seconds the code lives; default 300.

methods.description: Founder only. The code is single use and expires: `ttl_s` seconds (default 300, at most 600). The reply carries the listener certificate fingerprint and the address in `uri`, which is what the QR holds; a client pins that fingerprint and refuses any other certificate. It is not replayed by request_id: a retry with the same request_id runs again and makes another code.
methods.x-note: The code is shown once and kept only as a hash; a second call makes a new code and leaves the first valid until it expires or is used.

methods.name: device.redeem
methods.summary: Trade a pairing code for a device token.
methods.description: The only method an unpaired network caller may call. A code that is wrong, expired or already used is refused, gate `pairing_code`, without saying which; too many wrong tries are refused, gate `attempt_limit`. A code redeems once: the token is in this one reply and never again, and the daemon keeps only its hash. `name` is how the device is listed. It is not replayed by request_id either: a retry runs again, and a code that was redeemed stays used, so the retry is refused. The wrong-code count for a redeem over the local socket is kept under the host '' (the empty string), since it has no address.

methods.name: device.revoke
methods.summary: Cancel a device and close its connections at once.
methods.description: Cancels the device's token. Its open connections and terminal attaches are closed at once, its next call is refused (gate `unpaired`), and a device.revoked event is sent on the devices topic. Revoking a device that is not paired is not_found.

AgentName.description: An agent's name, as hl team lists it.

Role.description: Ordered lowest to highest. A method's role is the lowest that may call it; every higher role may too.

Topic.description: chat is added for the chat view (the UI design update): messages, landing state, transcript items and working state of one agent; events carry `agent`. devices (founder only, subscribed on its own, live only): pairing and revocation of devices. hr: HR proposals, so a client's tab dot is live; any proven caller, as hr.list. transcript: the per-agent event stream of a structured session (transcript.event), served only for an agent the daemon runs as a structured session; see the Transcript stream section.

name.description: The user, the device's name, or the agent's name.

device.description: Device id, when kind is device.

Actor.description: Who did a write; recorded on its event.

said.description: One sentence for a person, the legacy `said`.

replayed.description: True when this is the stored reply to a retried request_id; the action was not repeated.

Accepted.description: Every write's result. A refusal is the `refused` error, never an accepted:false result.

gate.description: Stable id of the gate that refused; see x-gates.

hint.description: The command or step that fixes it, when there is one.

proposal.description: With gates proposal_changed and proposal_settled: the proposal as it is now.

plan.description: With gate confirm: what the call would do and who is told.

id.description: Opaque; changes whenever the open prompt changes (the daemon uses the screen block's fingerprint).

kind.description: permission, question, dialog or exit_confirm today; open set. A dialog is `dialog` unless its screen is a known one (contract/prompts/).

oneOf.description: The tool asking, when the screen's title names a known one or the hook record does; else null.
The command or action it wants to run, as the screen shows it; null when the screen states none.
Why it asks, when the screen says; else null, never inferred.

lines.description: The dialog's panel as it is on screen, one string per line.

options.description: The choices, parsed from the dialog. Empty until the session-control task fills it; a client falls back to lines.

since.description: When the daemon first saw this prompt open.

multi.description: Several options may be picked, then submitted: prompt.answer takes `choice` as an array of PromptOption.key. Absent means false, as for every other prompt, where an array is bad_request.

role.description: The first line of the agent's ROLE.md that is not blank and not a heading, as one line, at most 160 characters; empty when there is none.

state.description: One of x-state-words, lower case; an open set, clients treat an unknown word as idle.

oneOf.description: Headline of what blocks it.

ctx_pct.description: Whole percent of the context window the agent's own session has used; null when it has no account, no session of its own, or a usage snapshot too old to trust. A view without the field is the same as null.

input_holders.description: Who holds the input; one in v1, a list so more can later. A structured agent has no input to hold: [].

state_detail.description: The text drawn beside the state word (a clock, what a wait is for), at most 40 characters; empty when there is none. The state column is drawn from state and state_detail alone.

started.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): whether the agent has ever run (a state row exists).

has_repo.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): whether its config names a repo.

has_terminal.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): whether a terminal is recorded for it.

screen_word.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): the word the screens draw for its state (RUNNING, IDLE, PENDING, MOVING, DIALOG, FATAL), `tui.screen_state`'s and not the wire `state`; null when it never started.

screen_detail.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): the text drawn beside screen_word.

unreached.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): requests, messages and answers owed to it that have not reached it.

words.description: The daemon's reason the task waits.

task_waits.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): its tasks that wait on a hold, oldest first.

wake_wait_reason.description: Only with agents.list `status: true` (what `hl team` draws): what holds back a wake that is due (set only while would_wake is true).

structured.description: The agent is set up to run as a structured session, whether its session is live or closed: the transcript topic and transcript.events serve it (the stored log too), chat.send returns a receipt for it, and it has no terminal to watch. Absent means false (a terminal agent), so a client needs no transcript.events probe to choose its view. Sent in agent.changed too.

kind.description: What the agent is, for a column (agents.kind): the model and its effort as `<model> <effort>`, effort one of low, mid, high, xhi, max (any other effort is shown whole), with the vendor in front as `<vendor> <model> <effort>` only when it is not claude. Absent from a daemon that does not serve it yet.

task_count.description: The tasks the agent owns that are not done: the current one and those waiting (queued or doing). A draft that is not the current task is not counted, as it is not approved yet; one the agent picked up and made current is. Absent from a daemon that does not serve it yet.

ready.description: The agent is idle (the screen word IDLE), has a current task, that task is queued, and no open blocker holds it: it can be given work now. Absent means false.

account.description: The account whose window the wake waits on.

clock.description: When that window rolls over, as unix seconds: the shortest walled window, the longest when only that stands. Null when the reset is not known or the wait is for a slot (the account is at its cap), not a window.

assumed.description: The account is a guess (nothing has confirmed the one the resume is tied to), not the account itself.

wall.description: What holds back a wake that is due (the screens' wall cell): the account that would wake it. Null when would_wake is false or nothing holds it back. Absent from a daemon that does not serve it yet.

fire.description: A trigger about to fire (the home row's warning cell): the daemon would hand this agent off at its next tick. `usage` is the shortest window at the wall, `usage_7d` the longest, `context` the context at its limit. Null when none, and for an agent whose triggers do not apply (closed, no terminal, parked, throttled or degraded). Needs a live evaluate over the agent's current usage and context readings, not a stored value. Absent from a daemon that does not serve it yet.

attention.description: What this agent alone asks of the founder, the most urgent of: `ask` (an open ask to the founder), `alert` (the screen word needs a human, or a delivery block the founder has been told of), `stuck` (a delivery that is not moving, or a usage limit), `running` (a turn is going on), in that order. Null when none. The daemon says nothing of folds, which are the screen's: a screen that hides some of an agent's reports (found through `parent`, all the way down) ranks `ask` first, then `alert` and `stuck` together, then `running`. It draws the mark of the first rank any of them has and counts those in that rank; `alert` and `stuck` share one mark and one count, red if any of them is `alert`, yellow otherwise (so one `alert` and one `stuck` make a red mark counting 2). Read from stored state, no live evaluate. Absent from a daemon that does not serve it yet.

cache_ignored.description: The agent's resume reuses its session whatever the prompt cache did (its own ignore_cache_expiry, else the global one), so a countdown from cache_until means nothing. Read from configuration. Absent means false.

config_error.description: Why the agent's configuration cannot be read, as one line; null when it can. When set, `kind` is absent (and the model, effort and the other fields that come from the configuration are null or absent). Absent from a daemon that does not serve it yet.

needs_you.description: Set while the agent waits on a decision only a person at its terminal can make. Fed by hooks (PermissionRequest and the permission and question Notification kinds) and by the session file's needs and tempo, never by reading the screen; cleared by the hook that follows (PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SessionEnd) or when the session file stops saying it. While set, `state` is `waiting`, `has_dialog` is true and `attention` is `alert`. null when none. Absent from a daemon that does not serve it yet (the Python daemon reads the screen and sets has_dialog and `alert` without it).

prompt.description: The agent's open prompt, or null.

cwd.description: The directory a shell command for this agent runs in: its worktree when that is on disk, else the daemon's home directory. worktree.path is what the agent's record holds and may name a directory that is gone; cwd is always usable.

can.description: Whether each action of the chat page's menu is worth offering now, by the daemon's own rules: ok, and why not when it is not.

Its deadline; null until the task is doing.

sandbox.description: Why a key, not an is_off/back_on pair: it is already an agent setting (agents.sandbox_on, `hl agent set sandbox=on`), read in AgentDetail.settings and written the same way as every other key. `on` takes effect at once (the key and the grant go now; a running session restarts on the next idle sweep). `off` needs the founder's grant.

active_cap.description: Default cap: most agents mid-turn at once on an account with no cap of its own.

ignore_cache_expiry.description: Resume the old session even after its cache went cold. Per agent with `agent`.

input_hold_idle_s.description: NEW, no code today: seconds a person or device may hold a terminal's input without typing before the daemon takes it back (see terminal `holder` notice).

MethodInfo.description: One method as a daemon lists it: its role and whether this caller may call it.

accounts.description: How many accounts have a reading.

oneOf.description: Percent of the week left, averaged over the accounts that have a reading at that time.

past.description: What usage samples recorded, oldest first.

oneOf.description: Percent of the week left, averaged over the accounts that have a reading at that time.

future.description: A guess: each account keeps its pace of the last day, and a week that resets starts again from nothing used. Kept apart from `past`, never joined to it.

oneOf.description: How long its headroom lasts at the current burn, whichever window runs out first; null when its reading is stale, there is no burn, or the window resets first.

agents.description: List-price cost in US dollars of each agent that day.

cost_per_day.description: Oldest first; a day with no calls is absent.

tokens.description: Tokens the agent used in the span.

cost.description: Its cost in US dollars at list price in the span, from the token log.

share.description: Its cost as a fraction (0 to 1) of everyone's cost in the span; 0 when nothing was spent.

est_pct.description: An estimate of the points of the combined week the agent used in the span: its cost share of each account times the points that account used, averaged over the accounts. An estimate, because what the plan charges is not what the price list says. Null when no account has a reading.

fracs.description: Its cost share of each account in the span, by account name (a fraction, 0 to 1). An account on which nothing at all was spent is absent; one on which others spent but none of this agent's tokens was priced is 0.

agent_use.description: What each agent used over the last `range` (the span of `past`), largest cost first, ties by name. A client groups agents by the first part of the dotted name; a group's numbers are the sums of its members' (est_pct null if any member's is). Absent from a daemon that does not send it.

overlay.description: Only with `agent`: the points of the combined week the pick had used by each time of `past`, one number per `past` entry in the same order: its cost share of each account times what that account had used so far, averaged over the accounts. Empty when the pick used nothing in the span or is not an agent or group. Absent from a daemon that does not send it.

seq.description: The last notice of this attach the screen includes; the next notice has seq+1.

data.description: Base64. Written unchanged to a freshly reset terminal of cols by rows, it paints the screen, the modes and the cursor.

alt_screen.description: The pane is on the alternate screen; data begins by switching to it.

cursor.description: 0-based column and row; also where data leaves the cursor.

holder.description: The first of holders; kept for clients written to the single value.

holders.description: Everyone who holds the input, oldest first; one in v1.

first.description: Absolute index of the first line, as in HistoryPage.

items.description: One physical row with its SGR codes: starts at default attributes and ends with a reset; no line break in it.

at.description: Where it sits in time: a request where its agent read it (landed_at) or else when it was made.

oneOf.description: request only: who dismissed it and why, when it was dismissed.
request only: the live state of the task a task delivery carries, else null.

change.description: task_event only: `queued -> doing`, `handed to X`, `assigned to X`, `title changed`, `priority 2 -> 1`. An open set: a client draws a word it does not know as text.

note.description: task_event only: the text typed with a handoff, else empty. Text from an agent.

oneOf.description: task_event only: the delivery a handoff belongs to, when it has one.

cause.description: session only: why a new conversation started (restart, wake, fresh close, move, handoff, launch). An open set.

oneOf.description: session only: the handoff record the session was given, else null.

CellColor.description: An xterm palette index (0-15 are the client's theme ANSI colours, 16-255 the fixed cube and greys) or a true colour as lower-case `#rrggbb`. A colour the cell does not have (the default) is left out, never sent as a number.

SpanStyle.description: Only what differs from the default cell: a flag is sent as true or left out, a colour is left out for the default. `inverse` is sent as the flag, not applied: the client swaps the foreground and background it draws, so default colours swap too. A client ignores a key it does not know.

error.description: Why the agent's `schedules` value cannot be read, as `hl schedule list` says it.

TranscriptEvent.description: One thing a structured session did, in order. Exactly the field named like `kind` is present besides the common ones (`text` for kind text). Events are never changed after they are sent.

session.description: The session id the event belongs to. A new session (a fresh start, not a resume) changes it; seq goes on.

seq.description: Per agent, starting at 1, up by exactly 1 with each event, across sessions, never reused. A client ignores an event whose seq is not above the last it applied and reads transcript.events on a hole.

oneOf.description: The uuid of the message that began the turn (the one chat.send's operation derives); null for an event outside a turn (an error at start).

kind.description: Open set: a client skips a kind it does not know.

oneOf.description: The id of the chat.transcript item the daemon also publishes for this event (kind text is a reply, permission is a prompt), so a view that shows both draws it once; null for a kind the chat view has no item for.

text.description: kind text: one whole assistant text block (no partial deltas in v1).

turn_start.description: kind turn_start: a message began a turn.

oneOf.description: Who sent it: a person, an agent, or the daemon.

tool_use.description: kind tool_use: the model called a tool.

id.description: The tool call's id; its tool_result and its permission carry it.

input.description: The tool's input as the model gave it.

tool_result.description: kind tool_result: what the tool returned.

text.description: At most 64 KiB; longer output is cut and `truncated` is true.

permission.description: kind permission: a person is asked. Answered by prompt.answer, with choice allow or deny.

prompt.description: kind permission; its id is tool_use_id; options are allow and deny; `reason` is the CLI's decision_reason.

permission_answer.description: kind permission_answer: a tool call was allowed or denied. A call a policy decides has this event alone, with no permission before it.

by.description: person: prompt.answer. policy: the rule named in `rule`. cancel: the CLI withdrew the prompt. closed: the session closed or no handler answered (fail closed: deny).

oneOf.description: The policy rule that matched, when by is policy.
The text the model saw with a deny.

turn_end.description: kind turn_end: the turn is over.

error.description: kind error: the session or the CLI failed; a turn_end follows if a turn was running.

more.description: There are more in the direction asked.

first_seq.description: The oldest seq the daemon still keeps for the agent; 0 when it has none.

last_seq.description: The newest seq of the agent; 0 when it has none.

gap.description: since_seq was older than first_seq - 1: the read starts at first_seq, and what lay between is gone.

state.description: queued: held by the daemon behind a running turn, not written to the CLI. sent: written to the CLI, not yet echoed. confirmed: the CLI echoed the message's uuid. unknown: written, and the daemon or the CLI ended before the echo; never written again.

uuid.description: The message's uuid, derived by the daemon from the request_id; the id the transcript stream's turn_start carries. Read it, do not compute it.

seq.description: The seq of the transcript event that carries this uuid, when there is one; absent otherwise (a message that joined a running turn has no turn_start of its own). Best effort; a client does not wait for it.

Receipt.description: Where a message to a structured agent is on its way into the CLI. Only for an agent whose AgentView.structured is true; see x-delivery.

terminal.description: The terminal handle, as terminal.attach takes it.

kind.description: permission: a tool or a folder waits for a yes. question: the agent asked the person something. usage: the session limit's choice. dialog: any other, and any the daemon does not know: unknown is a person.

text.description: One line, from the hook or the session file; never read from the screen.

source.description: hook: PermissionRequest or Notification. session: the session's own file (sessions/<pid>.json needs, tempo).

bad_request.data: {code, field?, method?}; also JSON-RPC parse errors (-32700), invalid params (-32602) and an unknown method (-32601, data.method).

daemon_down.data: {code, log_path}; raised by the client library, never sent on the wire.

x-transcript.what: The per-agent stream a view draws for a structured session (the CLI's frames reduced to what a view needs), in place of a terminal. Topic `transcript`, event type `transcript.event`, data TranscriptEvent; events carry `agent`, so subscribe's `agent` filters. `hello.capabilities.transcript` says the daemon serves it; `AgentView.structured` says which agents it serves it for (absent: a terminal agent, whose transcript.events is refused, gate unsupported, and whose terminal a client shows). The topic needs member, as transcript.events does: subscribe naming it from an agent session is refused, gate role.
x-transcript.kinds: turn_start (a message began a turn: uuid, sender, text), text (one whole assistant text block), tool_use (id, tool, input), tool_result (tool_use_id, ok, text cut at 64 KiB), permission (a person is asked: a Prompt), permission_answer (allowed or denied, and by whom), turn_end (reason, cost_usd, duration_ms, usage), error (code, text). The order within a turn: turn_start, then text, tool_use, permission, permission_answer and tool_result as they happen, then turn_end. A tool_result follows its tool_use, not necessarily next. Open set: a client skips a kind it does not know.
x-transcript.permission: A tool call that needs a person is a `permission` event whose `prompt` is an ordinary Prompt: kind permission, id = the tool call's id, options `allow` and `deny`, tool, command and reason as for any prompt. The card calls prompt.answer with choice allow or deny, and prompt.list holds it while it is open (it is also in the chat view as a prompt item and in the inbox, as today). The `permission_answer` event ends it, whoever answered: `by` person (prompt.answer), policy (a rule decided; no `permission` came before), cancel (the CLI withdrew it) or closed (the session closed or no handler answered: deny). A client that reconnects and sees a permission with no answer after it asks prompt.list before showing buttons.
x-transcript.sequence: `seq` is per agent, starts at 1, goes up by exactly 1 with each event, continues across sessions of the agent (the `session` field changes on a fresh start, not on a resume) and is never reused. Events are final: nothing is changed after it is sent.
x-transcript.resume: The connection's cursor works as for every topic: subscribe with `since` replays what was missed, up to the usual 5000 events, in full. A client that has no cursor, or gets `gap`, or sees a seq that is not last + 1, reads transcript.events: first load with no since_seq (the newest page), older pages with before_seq, the missed ones with since_seq = the last seq it applied. To start without a race: subscribe first, then read, then apply stream events above the read's last_seq and drop those at or below the last it holds. `gap: true` in the read means the daemon no longer keeps the events between; the client shows the break and goes on from first_seq.
x-transcript.send: A message goes in by chat.send with the client's own request_id as its operation id (see x-delivery); the daemon derives the message uuid from it, so the `turn_start` event for a message that begins a turn carries the uuid. A message that joined a running turn has no turn_start. chat.messages has the message under the same operation, with its receipt.
x-transcript.chat: chat.transcript is unchanged and stays the chat view's feed: a `text` event is also a reply item and a `permission` also a prompt item (the event's `item` is that item's id, so a view showing both draws it once); tool_use, tool_result, turn_start, turn_end and error have no chat item, and chat.transcript has still no tool item. The task_event and session items exist only in chat.transcript. A view that renders the transcript uses this stream and ignores chat.transcript's reply and prompt items for the same agent.
x-transcript.not_in_v1: Partial text deltas, thinking blocks, images, and the edit diff of a tool. A tool's input is whatever the model sent.

x-delivery.what: How a message reaches a structured agent, and what the composer shows. One path serves a person, an agent, the daemon's own notices and a task; the apps use it through chat.send.
x-delivery.operation: The caller's request_id is the operation id. The daemon derives the message uuid from it, records the operation before writing, and answers a repeat with the recorded operation without writing again. A client makes a new request_id for each message it means to send and keeps it across retries of that one message.
x-delivery.receipt: Receipt.state: queued (held behind a running turn), sent (written to the CLI), confirmed (the CLI echoed the uuid), unknown (see crash rule). The order is queued, sent, confirmed; unknown follows sent. `accepted` is never `delivered`: a caller that needs delivery waits for confirmed, with its own deadline. There is no `published` state: a message that joins a running turn has no turn_start, so `seq` on the receipt is optional and best effort.
x-delivery.repeat: The same request_id and params returns {accepted, replayed: true, request, receipt} with the receipt as it is now, so a retry after a lost reply learns whether the message was echoed. The same request_id with other params is bad_request. This is the one write whose replay is not the first reply frozen.
x-delivery.delivery: chat.send `delivery`: queue (default) or now. Queue while a turn runs is held by the daemon, which persists it, and is written when the CLI reports the turn over. Now is written at once and joins the running turn. With nothing running both are written at once and the receipt is sent.
x-delivery.crash: If the daemon or the CLI ends with an operation sent and not confirmed, the daemon does not write it again: the operation is unknown, the sender is told (the chat event), and it stays unknown. A queued operation survives and is written after the restart. A person who sees unknown may chat.send the text again under a NEW request_id (their call: the CLI may have run it); chat.cancel keeps its meaning for a delivered message. Nothing else changes an unknown operation.
x-delivery.queued: chat.send_now writes a queued operation now, with priority now (receipt sent). chat.cancel withdraws it without confirm. Both are refused (gate state) for any other receipt; there is no chat.withdraw.
x-delivery.view: ChatMessage.receipt carries the receipt, and landing follows it: queued is queued, sent and unknown are typed (sending_reason says unknown), confirmed is delivered. Each change sends the usual chat.message event. A terminal agent's message has no receipt.
x-delivery.terminal: An agent whose AgentView.structured is not true accepts `delivery` and ignores it, and its result and messages have no receipt.

x-structured-controls.what: How the apps drive and watch an agent that AgentView.structured marks. It has no terminal: everything below is a chat, session or prompt call.
x-structured-controls.watch: transcript.events and the transcript topic show what it did; chat.transcript and chat.messages draw the conversation and each message's receipt. Both stay readable while its session is closed.
x-structured-controls.detail: agent.get: terminal null, session_open true while its session is live, input_holders [].
x-structured-controls.controls: session.start, wake, restart, park, stop (exit and close are the same; kill is for a person) and interrupt (refused, gate state, when no turn runs); prompt.answer takes allow or deny; chat.send, chat.send_now and chat.cancel as in Delivery.
x-structured-controls.never: A client does not send session.input, session.keys, session.type, input.take, input.release or terminal.attach for a structured agent, and shows no terminal tab, holder, key strip or Take control. The Go daemon does not serve the first five at all; a daemon that does refuses a structured agent (gate unsupported). terminal.attach with agent is not_found (terminal): it has no terminal.
